scenes.heading: Kappa Architecture
scenes.narration: The Kappa architecture treats every workload as a stream, processing all data through a single streaming pipeline and eliminating Lambda's separate batch layer.

scenes.heading: Core ideas
bullets: One code path for real-time and reprocessing
An immutable, replayable log is the source of truth
Reprocess by replaying the log through a new job
No dual batch and speed layers to sync
scenes.narration: Kappa uses a single stream-processing code path for both live data and historical reprocessing, so you write and maintain your logic only once. It relies on a durable, replayable log such as Kafka as the system of record. To reprocess history or fix a bug, you simply replay the log through a new version of the job and swap outputs. This removes the burden of keeping duplicate batch and speed layers in sync that plagues Lambda.

scenes.heading: Reprocessing in Kappa
steps: Immutable events stored in the log
Start a new job from log start
Swap serving output when caught up
scenes.narration: All events are retained in an immutable, replayable log. The streaming job consumes that log and continuously produces results. When you discover a bug or need new logic, you do not run a separate batch job; instead you start a fresh instance of the job that reads the log from the beginning. Once that new job catches up to the present, you atomically switch the serving layer to its output and retire the old version.

scenes.heading: Kappa vs Lambda
scenes.narration: Kappa keeps a single streaming code path, which makes it simpler to operate and reason about, but it requires the log to retain enough history to support full replays. Lambda splits work into batch and speed layers, which duplicates logic and adds operational overhead, but the dedicated batch layer can be more efficient for reprocessing very large historical datasets. Kappa has become the default for many modern platforms as streaming engines and cheap log storage have matured.

scenes.heading: What Kappa requires to work
bullets: A durable, replayable log as source of truth
A stream engine with exactly-once semantics
scenes.narration: Kappa places real demands on your infrastructure. It needs a durable, replayable log such as Kafka to serve as the immutable source of truth. That log must retain enough history, sometimes offloaded to cheap object storage, so a job can replay from far enough back. It needs a stream-processing engine that offers exactly-once semantics so replays do not double-count. And it relies on stateful processing with checkpointing so long-running aggregations survive restarts and can resume cleanly.

scenes.heading: Where Kappa struggles
bullets: Very large historical reprocessing can be slow
Some batch-only algorithms are awkward in streams
scenes.narration: Kappa is not a silver bullet. Replaying years of history through a streaming job can be slower than a purpose-built batch job would be. Retaining that much log data costs storage, even when tiered to cheap object stores. Some algorithms that assume a bounded, complete dataset are awkward to express as continuous streams. And large backfills can place heavy, spiky load on the same cluster that serves live traffic, so you must plan capacity carefully.

scenes.text: When your engine can both stream and replay, Kappa gives you one pipeline to build, test, and trust.
scenes.narration: When your streaming engine can handle both live processing and full historical replay, Kappa lets you build, test, and trust a single pipeline instead of maintaining two, which is why it is often the simpler modern choice.
